tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Recognition, recall, description and guided application (understand and identify).

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: No prior experience of treating creativity as an academic skill is assumed. The learner is early in their studies and may believe creativity is an artistic gift that some people have and others do not, or that it has no place in their subject; teach from first principles.

subThemes.label: Creativity is a developable skill, not an innate artistic gift possessed by a few
What creativity means in academic work: generating novel ideas, making unexpected connections, approaching a problem from several angles
Divergent thinking (generating many possibilities) versus convergent thinking (narrowing to the best)
How creativity and critical thinking work together: creativity generates ideas, critical thinking evaluates them
Common barriers to creativity: fear of failure, perfectionism, and the pressure to be right first time
Giving yourself permission to produce rough or 'bad' ideas as a route to good ones

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, creativity as a skill: what the word really means at university. Second, divergent and convergent thinking: the two modes behind creative work. Third, getting past the barriers: what blocks creativity and how to move through it. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about creativity at university: what it really means and why it matters in every subject. By the end you will be able to explain that creativity is a skill you can build, tell divergent thinking apart from convergent thinking, and recognise the barriers that get in the way.

Creativity is not only for artists or for people who feel naturally inventive. Generating ideas, making unexpected connections and approaching a problem from several angles are things every student does, and every student can get better at.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain creativity as a developable skill, distinguish divergent from convergent thinking, recognise the barriers and how to work past them.

practiceConnection.academic: Creativity is a habit academic work rewards far more than students expect. Every essay that asks for an argument of your own, every project that needs a fresh angle, every problem without a set answer draws on the same skill. Build it now and it carries into every module of your degree.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced creativity courses take the skill into creative methods for real study tasks, and then into innovation, enterprise and professional practice. Going wider: the same habits underpin Criticality, Reflective Practice and Researching, where you put creative thinking to work alongside other skills.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Creativity is no longer a vague gift that belongs to other people: it is a skill you can describe and begin to build. You can explain that creativity is developable and matters in every subject. You can tell divergent thinking, which generates ideas, apart from convergent thinking, which chooses among them. And you can name the barriers, such as fear of failure and perfectionism, and a move that loosens each.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, creativity is something you practise in every module. Each time you generate options before choosing, each unexpected connection you follow, each rough idea you let live long enough to grow, is the skill at work. It is also what professional life rewards: finding fresh angles and turning ideas into action travels well beyond your degree.
